author: James Mertz
title: 'There's not too many people that can really guard me': Tariq Francis speaks after setting program record - The Daily Targum
text:
With his 29 points on Wednesday night, junior guard Tariq Francis set a program record for the most points for a Rutgers men’s basketball player in a Big Ten Tournament game. He spoke to the media about his performance, the season-saving win and more.
“Just staying with the game plan,” Francis said. “So just running the plays correctly, try to keep the attention to detail.”
Francis found a lot of his success in the first half when the Scarlet Knights' offense was very stagnant, and he played hero ball late in the shot clock. He racked up 16 points in the first half, good for more than half of the team’s points.
“I try to balance looking for an angle to score as well as what my teammates are doing,” Francis said. “They do a great job moving off the ball. So if I could always snap passes to them and they could get a shot, like [Zrno] or any of those guys, I try to do that, but if I can get a shot up, I’ll try to.”
Of those 16 points in the opening half, 12 of them came from the three-ball. He went 4-of-5 from beyond the arc in the first half, knocking down five for the game, the most he’s had this season.
“Shooting with confidence,” Francis said. “Me and coach Pikiell we had a good talk, and he was just telling me, ‘don’t hesitate, if I get good looks, take them’ because it's better than trying to do a lot of other stuff, which may waste energy and be tougher than just an open three-pointer.”
Along with Francis’ scoring, the Rutgers bench combined for 21 points of its own, completely mismatching Minnesota in that regard.
“They gave us great energy,” Francis said. “Everybody that played just came in and gave us energy, and we knew that [Minnesota] had less players and they played less players…being able to play connected and stay together was important for us.”
Francis made it clear that in a certain aspect of the game, there is just nobody better.
“I feel like offensively, 1-on-1, there's not too many people that can really guard me,” he said.
